clinicalPearls: Defined by the tetrad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
In children it is most often idiopathic, and minimal change disease is the predominant histology, especially in preschool children.
Oedema is the usual presenting feature, typically starting periorbitally and becoming generalised with dependent swelling and sometimes ascites.
Most childhood cases are steroid-responsive, so an empirical corticosteroid trial is standard first-line therapy without initial biopsy in the typical age group.
Renal biopsy is reserved for atypical features: older or very young age, gross haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance.
Children are at increased risk of infection (notably pneumococcal peritonitis) from urinary immunoglobulin loss, and of thromboembolism from a hypercoagulable state.
Supportive care includes sensible salt restriction, careful management of oedema, and attention to nutrition and infection prevention including vaccination.
Relapses are common; the pattern of response guides classification into steroid-sensitive, frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Injury to the glomerular filtration barrier, particularly the podocytes and their slit diaphragms, increases permeability to plasma proteins, producing heavy albuminuria. In minimal change disease, light microscopy is near-normal and electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, implicating a circulating permeability factor and immune dysregulation. Urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and, together with secondary sodium retention, causing oedema. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, producing hyperlipidaemia. Loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors predisposes to infection, and loss of anticoagulant proteins with raised procoagulants predisposes to thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Oedema from cardiac, hepatic, or nutritional causes
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or timed collection)
Serum albumin, total protein, and lipid profile
Complement levels and autoimmune serology when nephritic features are present
Renal biopsy in atypical or steroid-resistant cases
redFlags: Fever with abdominal pain suggesting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, respiratory distress, neurological signs)
Hypertension, gross haematuria, or reduced renal function suggesting a nephritic process
Severe hypovolaemia from rapid fluid shifts, or tense ascites and respiratory compromise
Steroid resistance prompting reassessment and biopsy
reference.prognosis: Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have a good long-term renal outcome despite frequent relapses; steroid resistance, often from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Attributing oedema to another cause and missing proteinuria on urinalysis
Overlooking infection or thrombosis, the major acute complications
Missing atypical features that warrant biopsy rather than empirical steroids
Aggressive diuresis precipitating hypovolaemia and thrombosis in an intravascularly depleted child
